text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft this, one concern about the guest score claim. Your GM approved the lobby and room renovation and knows it happened in the same 18 months. If the page says you're the main reason scores went up, the GM is likely to think of the renovation first, and that could make them doubt the rest of the page. The case can still use the score. It needs evidence tying the rise to the front desk, and that's what the first question below is after.

1. **Is there anything that separates the front desk's effect on the score from the renovation's?** For example: when did your new training start, compared with when the score began rising and when the renovation finished? Do reviews mention staff, speed or friendliness more often now? Does the review site give separate scores for staff or service?
2. **Have you done any work close to budgeting?** Building schedules, controlling labour hours or overtime, approving timecards, or watching payroll against forecast during the 7 weeks you've been covering? If not, would you commit to a plan to learn it, such as training with the controller or the GM?
3. **What happened during those 7 weeks?** Did scores, staffing or overtime hold steady or improve? Did you handle anything hard, like a big group, a staff problem or an audit?
4. **What does your GM care about most right now, and what doubts might they have about you?** Examples: cost control, reviews, the budget gap, or whether you're ready to manage people who used to be your peers.
5. **Do you know what turnover costs per hire, or why people used to leave?** Even a rough figure like "about $X per hire to recruit and train," or "exit interviews mentioned poor training," would make the turnover drop count for more.

If you don't know some of these, say so. I'll write around the gaps and won't make anything up.

1. The renovation started 5 months into the 18 months. The check-in score had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started. I don't know exactly how the training timing lines up, whether reviews mention staff more, or whether the site has a separate staff score. If "main reason" goes too far, I'm fine with just saying what I did.

2. During the 7 weeks, overtime came in under the monthly plan. I'll commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (the company pays for it). I'll also do weekly sessions on the payroll budget with our controller, Ben Oduya, who has already offered.

3. No front desk shift went uncovered in those 7 weeks, and overtime was under plan. I don't know how scores moved in that period, and nothing big comes to mind.

4. Probably the budget gap. There's also an outside candidate with experience at a larger hotel, and I can't match that. And Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at the desk, so that could come up.

5. I don't know either one.

<final_document>
**To:** [GM name]
**From:** [Your name], Assistant Front Office Manager
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** My application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the Front Office Manager role. For the past seven weeks I've been doing the whole job on my own. The case for me rests on that, and on six years at this desk.

**I've already been doing the job**
Since [previous FOM's name] left, I've run the front office alone. In those seven weeks no front desk shift has gone uncovered, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan. You wouldn't have to wait for a new manager to learn the role, because the work is already getting done.

**What I've changed at the desk**
- **Training.** I rewrote our front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- **Turnover.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 of 14 left.
- **Guest scores.** Our check-in score on [review site] rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the past 18 months. The renovation clearly helped. But the score had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 in the five months before work began, so part of the rise came from the desk itself.

**What I bring that an outside hire can't**
An outside candidate may have run a bigger operation than I have. What I have is six years at this hotel. I know our team, our systems, our regular guests and our weak spots. The staff I'd be managing are people I trained, and many of them have stayed. An outside hire would need months to learn what I already know.

**The budget**
I haven't owned a budget, and I know the $1.1 million payroll budget is a big part of this role. My plan for it:
- Finish the company's finance course within my first three months.
- Meet weekly with Ben Oduya on the payroll budget. He has already offered.
- Keep controlling overtime as I have for the last seven weeks, when it came in under plan.

**My first priority**
Friday evening check-in waits are still our most common complaint at the desk. Fixing them would be my first job as Front Office Manager. Within my first 30 days I'll bring you a staffing and process plan to cut those waits.

I'd welcome the chance to talk this through before you decide.

[Your name]
</final_document>

A few notes on the draft:

- **Guest scores:** It doesn't say you're the main reason scores went up. Your GM will remember the renovation, so that claim would probably hurt you. Instead the memo points out that the score went from 7.9 to 8.2 before the renovation started. That's true, and it does more for you. It still doesn't say your training caused that early rise, because we don't know when the training started.
- **Turnover:** The memo gives the before and after numbers without saying your training caused the drop. Your GM can make that connection. If they ask why people stopped leaving, you can answer then.
- **Check before Friday:** The memo commits you to a 30-day plan for the Friday evening waits. Take that line out if you can't deliver it. Also fill in the placeholders and get Ben Oduya's OK before naming him.
